title: Contrasting trophic cascades generated by a community of generalist predators
species: Cucumis sativus (cucumber, var. Spacemaster) and Cucumis pepo (squash, var. Yellow Crookneck)
location: University of Kentucky Spindletop Research Farm, Fayette County, Kentucky, USA
design: Factorial manipulation of ground predator (carabid beetle and lycosid spider) immigration into fenced 8x8m vegetable plots plus unfenced reference plots. Five treatments: O (fenced, neither carabid nor lycosid immigration allowed), C (fenced, carabid immigration only), L (fenced, lycosid immigration only), C+L (fenced, both carabid and lycosid immigration), OPEN (unfenced reference plots, natural immigration). 36-cm metal drift fences blocked ground predator immigration; pitfall traps regulated densities within fenced plots. Carabids and lycosids were added to treatment plots at mean natural immigration rates. Two sequential crops each year: spring cucumber (planted June), summer squash (planted late July). 1997: 20 plots in RCBD (4 per treatment). 1998: 25 new plots in CRD (5 per treatment). ANOVA: 2x2x2 factorial (year x carabid x lycosid) for fenced treatments; OPEN compared informally. No pesticides or fertilizers applied.
notes: This is a factorial addition/exclusion experiment. The O treatment (no predators, fenced) serves as the 'excluded' arm for the meta-analysis PICO, and OPEN (unfenced, natural predator immigration) serves as the control. The design is primarily an addition experiment (predators added into predator-free fenced plots), but the O vs OPEN comparison functions as an exclusion experiment. n=4 plots per treatment in 1997 (RCBD), n=5 in 1998 (CRD). The paper's formal ANOVA uses only the fenced treatments in a 2x2x2 factorial; O vs OPEN is an informal comparison. The paper verifies fence artifact was minimal: C+L and OPEN did not differ significantly for most outcomes (P>0.10), except squash yield in 1997 where OPEN had nearly zero production, likely due to vertebrate seed predators or herbivores destroying squash in open plots (the fence excluded vertebrates as well as ground arthropods). Carabids and lycosids had contrasting and seasonally variable effects: in spring cucumber, lycosids increased yield (F=8.60, P=0.007) while carabids had no significant effect (P=0.15); in summer squash, carabids increased yield (F=13.40, P=0.001) but lycosids decreased yield (F=9.26, P=0.005), likely via intraguild predation on nabid bugs, important squash bug predators. All yield data from Fig 5 only (no tabulated numeric means). Pest abundance data exists in Figs 6-9 for striped cucumber beetles, squash bugs, and nabid bugs by treatment, but is not extracted here as the O vs OPEN pest comparisons are confounded by fence effects and are not formally tested in the paper.

figure_read.structure: Two panels (A: cucumber, B: squash). Five treatment groups on x-axis: O, C, L, C+L, OPEN. Two bars per group: 1997 (lighter/white) and 1998 (darker/gray). Y-axis 'Fruit Production (kg/plot)', ticks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; spacing 10; unit kg/plot; linear. Caption states error bars are +1 SE. O = no predators; OPEN = unfenced reference.
figure_read.evidence_note: Fig 5A p7; O treatment 1997 (light bar); bar top sits ~80% of the way from 0 to the 10 tick, so ~8 kg/plot. Error bar cap extends to ~12, so SE ~4. OPEN 1997 bar: top sits ~80% between 20 and 30 ticks, so ~28 kg/plot; SE ~5. Direction: excluding ground predators strongly reduces cucumber yield — consistent with expected biocontrol effect. This is the largest yield effect in the paper. Scanned figure; readings approximate to ±2 kg/plot.

observations.notes: 1997 had substantially higher cucumber yields than 1998 across all treatments (F=8.92, P=0.005), making the absolute effect size much larger in 1997. Treatment SE ~4 kg/plot (error bar extends from ~8 to ~12). Control SE ~5 (from ~28 to ~33). The paper's formal ANOVA is a 2x2x2 factorial among fenced treatments only (OPEN excluded); the lycosid main effect is significant (F=8.60, P=0.007), carabid main effect is not (P=0.15), and no year x treatment interactions are significant (P>0.27). The O vs OPEN comparison is informal but represents the cleanest exclusion-vs-natural contrast. Cucumber harvested July 16, 1997 (subsample of 14 plants/plot from 2 plants per row x 7 rows). The fence also excludes vertebrate seed predators/herbivores, but the paper notes C+L ≈ OPEN for cucumber yield (P>0.10), so the fence artifact is minimal for this crop.

figure_read.structure: Panel B of Fig 5 (squash). Five treatment groups: O, C, L, C+L, OPEN. Two bars per group (1997, 1998). Y-axis 'Fruit Production (kg/plot)', ticks at 0, 5, 10, 15; spacing 5; linear. Error bars +1 SE.
figure_read.evidence_note: Fig 5B p7; O treatment 1997 (light bar); bar top at the 5 tick. SE ~2 (error bar to ~7). OPEN 1997 bar: barely visible above zero, ~0.5-1 kg/plot. Near-zero OPEN value makes this comparison unreliable — see notes. Direction is OPPOSITE expected: excluding predators produced more squash than open plots. This is confounded by vertebrate damage.

observations.notes: CAUTION: This comparison is confounded. OPEN squash yield was nearly zero in 1997, likely because vertebrate seed predators or herbivores (mice, birds, rabbits) destroyed squash plants in unfenced plots — the 36-cm fences that excluded ground arthropods also excluded vertebrates. The paper explicitly discusses this: 'It is possible that vertebrate seed predators or herbivores... destroyed squash plants in the open gardens in that first year; fencing would have retarded the entry of many vertebrates.' Alternatively, the paper notes that higher lycosid densities in OPEN in 1997 may have indirectly elevated squash bug densities (via intraguild predation on nabid bugs). This observation should not be interpreted as evidence that ground predator exclusion benefits squash yield. The effect direction was checked and re-checked — it reflects the confounded fence effect, not a predator-exclusion effect. Squash harvested Sep 15, 1997.

observations.notes: 1998 squash data is a cleaner comparison than 1997 because OPEN plots produced normally (vertebrate interference not apparent). Squash yield was significantly higher in 1998 than 1997 (F=5.00, P=0.03). Within the factorial, carabids significantly increased squash yield (F=13.40, P=0.001) but lycosids significantly decreased it (F=9.26, P=0.005), with additive effects (interaction P=0.92). The lycosid negative effect on squash yield is attributed to intraguild predation: lycosids preyed on nabid bugs (key squash bug predators), indirectly increasing squash bug densities and reducing squash production. Treatment SE ~1. Control SE ~1.5. Squash harvested Sep 8, 1998.
